subject: probability of observing object in defined area?

messages.author: 19ed026c75ce9993
messages.subject: probability of observing object in defined area?
parts:
Essentially, my question is this:
If the value of p, the probability of observing an
object in defined area, equals 1.00 within a given
radius (truncation point), would it be legitimate to
assume that a complete census has taken place within
this area?

I am using point count data and program DISTANCE to
estimate and compare densities of songbirds in four
cover types. In order to make these comparisons among
cover types, I partitioned the data among each of the
four cover type prior to analysis. I have been able to
obtain densities for some bird species in some cover
types, but limitations in sample sizes have prevented me
from effectively using DISTANCE to obtain densities in
other cover types. (Note: I used a cutoff of n=40 for
DISTANCE analysis).
If, for a given species in a given cover type, the
maximum distance (area) in which p=1.00 were obtained by
incrementally truncating the data until p=1.00. Could
this area then be used to calculate a density for the
same species in a less complex cover type? In other
words, divide the number of observations of a species
within this p=1.00 distance in cover type A, by the area
defined by p=1.00 for the same species in cover type B.
